name: Lisbon
info: Lisbon is the capital of Portugal, on the northern shore of the Tagus estuary in the west of the Iberian Peninsula, an Iron Age and Roman port that became the seat of an Atlantic trading empire.

facts.founded: Iron Age people occupied the Castelo hill from the 8th to 6th centuries BCE and traded with the Phoenicians; a legend names the mythical Ulysses as founder.
facts.where: On the northern shore of the Tagus, near its mouth, in the western part of the Iberian Peninsula, in present-day Portugal.
facts.known: The Roman port of Olisipo; Muslim al-Us̲h̲būna; the conquest of 1147; the capital of Portugal; the departure of Portuguese voyages of discovery; the spice and slave trades; the earthquake of 1755; the Pombaline Baixa
facts.today: Lisbon is the capital and most populous city of Portugal.

t: Lisbon grew from an Iron Age settlement on the Castelo hill that traded with the Phoenicians into the Roman municipium of Olisipo and, after the 8th century, the Muslim city of al-Us̲h̲būna, which Afonso I conquered in 1147.

It became the capital of Portugal in the 13th century and, from the end of the 15th century, the port from which most Portuguese expeditions set out, trading in spices, slaves, sugar and textiles between Africa, India, the Far East and Brazil.
The earthquake of 1 November 1755 destroyed 85 percent of its buildings, and the lower town was rebuilt on a rectangular plan under the Marquis of Pombal.
dyk: Pombal's planners tested architectural models for the rebuilt Baixa by having troops march around them to simulate an earthquake.

sections.origins:
Lisbon stands on the northern shore of the Tagus, close to its mouth, in the western part of the Iberian Peninsula. The estuary's sheltered harbour, the Mar da Palha, has been called the best natural port on the Atlantic coast of Portugal. In the Neolithic period pre-Celtic peoples built megaliths, dolmens and menhirs, some of which survive on the edge of the city, and permanent settlements do not appear in the archaeological record until about 2500 BCE. Celts entered the peninsula in the 1st millennium BCE and mixed with the earlier population, giving rise to Celtic-speaking tribes such as the Cempsi and the Sefes.

Archaeological finds show that Iron Age people occupied the Castelo hill from the 8th to 6th centuries BCE and traded with the Phoenicians, which accounts for the Phoenician pottery found there. A Phoenician trading post stood on the southern slope of the hill, and the settlement exchanged metals, salt and salted fish from the inland tribes for Phoenician goods. Most modern historians believe that Lisbon began as an indigenous settlement with commercial ties to the Phoenicians rather than as a Phoenician foundation. The first fortifications on the hill are no older than the 2nd century BCE.

The origin of the name is unknown. Latin and Greek writers called the city Olisipo, Olissipo or Ulyssippo and repeated a legend that the hero Ulysses founded it. The Phoenician derivation Alis Ubbo, "safe harbour", has no evidence behind it and is never attested in classical literature.
sections.growth:
Under Rome the city, called Olisipo, prospered as piracy was suppressed. It traded with Britannia, particularly Cornwall, and with the Rhine, and was known for garum, a fish sauce exported to Rome, and for wine, salt and horse-breeding. In the reign of Augustus the Romans built a theatre, the Cassian Baths, temples and a large forum. A broad road linked it to Bracara Augusta and Emerita Augusta, the capital of Lusitania.

After the conquest of 1147 Afonso I granted Lisbon a charter in 1179 and set up a fair to restore its commerce. Portuguese merchants, Christian and Jewish, traded with Seville, Southampton, Bruges and the Hanseatic cities, and a maritime judicial office, the Alcaide do Mar, was created in 1242. The population was about 35,000 in 1300, 60,000 in 1400 and 70,000 in 1500.

Most Portuguese expeditions of the Age of Discovery set out from Lisbon between the end of the 15th century and the beginning of the 17th, among them Vasco da Gama's voyage to India in 1498. In the 16th century the city was the European hub of commerce between Africa, India, the Far East and later Brazil, and it grew rich on spices, slaves, sugar and textiles. The trading houses, among them the Casa da Índia, paid for the Jerónimos Monastery and the Belém Tower in the Manueline style. The population rose from 70,000 in 1528 to 120,000 in 1590 and was about 150,000 in 1600. In the early 18th century Brazilian gold allowed John V to sponsor Baroque churches and theatres.
sections.rulers:
Olisipo was integrated into the Roman empire in 138 BCE by the consul Decimus Junius Brutus Callaicus and became part of the province of Lusitania. Between 409 and 429 it was occupied in turn by Sarmatians, Alans and Vandals. The Suebi, whose kingdom had its capital at Bracara Augusta, controlled the region until 585, when their kingdom was absorbed into the Visigothic Kingdom of Toledo.

Muslim forces took the city in the early 8th century, and it came under the Umayyad Caliphate, then the Emirate of Córdoba and the Caliphate of Córdoba. For a brief time, from 1022 to 1034, it was the independent Taifa of Lisbon before the larger Taifa of Badajoz conquered it. Norwegian crusaders led by Sigurd I occupied it for three years from 1108, and the Almoravids took it in 1111. In 1147 Afonso I of Portugal laid siege to it and conquered it with the aid of crusader knights.

Lisbon replaced Coimbra as capital of the Portuguese territory in the 13th century. The succession crisis of 1580 began sixty years of dual monarchy with Spain under the Habsburgs, ended by a coup organised in Lisbon and carried out on 1 December 1640. From 1808 to 1821 the capital of the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves was Rio de Janeiro. King Carlos I was killed in Lisbon in 1908, a revolution on 5 October 1910 ended the monarchy, and the coup of 28 May 1926 began the Estado Novo, which lasted until 1974.
sections.life:
Roman Olisipo was ruled by an oligarchical council dominated by two families, the Julii and the Cassiae. Most of its people spoke Latin, with a large minority of Greek traders and slaves. Its first attested bishop was Potamius, around 356. Under Muslim rule the diverse population of Muwallads, Arabs, Berbers, Mozarabs, Saqaliba and Jews kept their own ways of life. Mozarabic was the native language of most Christians, Arabic was widely known, and Islam was the official religion. The city had a large mosque, a castle at the top of the hill, a medina and a fortress-palace for the governor, and the Alfama district grew beside the original core.

After 1147 the Muslims who remained were confined to the Mouraria, and the Jews, who may have made up about 10 percent of the population or more, were confined to three neighbourhoods called Judiarias. The Jews paid extra taxes, wore distinctive clothes and were forbidden to go out at night. Trades gathered in streets named for them, such as Rua do Ouro for the goldsmiths and Rua da Prata for the silversmiths. Merchants from Genoa, Venice and elsewhere formed communities in the city. By the mid-16th century ten percent of the population was of African descent.

King Denis founded the first Portuguese university in Lisbon in 1290, and it moved between Lisbon and Coimbra for many years before settling at Coimbra in the 16th century. The university was refounded in Lisbon in 1911. The first book printed in the city appeared in 1489. In the 16th century Luís de Camões, Gil Vicente, Pedro Nunes and Garcia da Orta lived there.
sections.crises:
The 1147 conquest was a bloody one. According to the chronicle of the siege, the local bishop was killed by the crusaders, and Muslims and Mozarabs were looted indiscriminately; most Muslims who did not convert fled, and all mosques were destroyed or converted into churches. A plague afterwards killed thousands of Mozarabs and Muslims. Earlier, in 844, Viking boats had sailed into the estuary and taken the city after a siege of 13 days, then retreated in the face of resistance by the townspeople.

The city suffered repeated earthquakes. One in 1290 was the first major quake in its recorded history, and eight were recorded in the 14th century. A famine in 1333 and the Black Death of 1348 killed half the population. Castile besieged the city in 1373 and left when it was paid a ransom, after which the Fernandine Walls were built. John I of Castile besieged it again in 1384, and the Portuguese under Nuno Álvares Pereira won. In 1506 a four-day riot by Old Christians killed several thousand New Christians. The plague of 1569 killed 50,000 people.

On 1 November 1755 an earthquake, followed by fires and a tsunami, killed an estimated 30,000 to 40,000 residents of a population estimated at between 200,000 and 275,000 and destroyed 85 percent of the city's structures, including the Ribeira Palace and the Hospital Real de Todos os Santos. Early in the 19th century many buildings were pillaged, sacked or destroyed by the Napoleonic invaders. In 1988 a fire in the Chiado destroyed many 18th-century Pombaline buildings.
sections.legacy:
After 1755 the Marquis of Pombal, minister of Joseph I, chose to demolish what remained of the medieval lower town and rebuild it on a rectangular plan with two great squares, the Praça do Rossio and the Praça do Comércio. The Baixa Pombalina is one of the first examples of earthquake-resistant construction: its buildings had a wood-lattice framework, the Pombaline cage, and inter-terrace walls higher than the roof timbers to check the spread of fires. The earthquake shocked Europe, and Voltaire wrote a long poem on it and mentioned it in Candide.

The Belém Tower and the Jerónimos Monastery, both Manueline, are listed as World Heritage Sites. The Alfama, whose name comes from the Arabic al-hamma, survived the earthquake with little damage because of its narrow streets. Lisbon has many examples of azulejo tile art, dating from the 15th century, and the Portuguese pavement, the calçada portuguesa, was born there in the mid-1800s.

During the Second World War Lisbon was one of the few neutral, open Atlantic ports of Europe, and more than 100,000 refugees fled Nazi Germany through it. The Carnation Revolution of 25 April 1974 ended the Estado Novo. Lisbon is today the capital and most populous city of Portugal, with about 658,000 people in the city and about 3.35 million in its metropolitan area.

summary: Lisbon, on the Tagus estuary, was an Iron Age port, the Roman Olisipo and the Muslim al-Us̲h̲būna before Afonso I conquered it in 1147. It became Portugal's capital in the 13th century, sent out the voyages of discovery, and was rebuilt after the earthquake of 1755.
